board_events.text: Lamarck (1809): organisms strive; what they practise in life is passed to their children. Disproved.
Darwin (1859): organisms vary at random; nature quietly selects the better-suited. Accepted, but incomplete.
Modern Synthesis (1942): Darwin's selection married to genetics. Currently accepted.
Then flip the question: what would a population look like if it were NOT evolving at all? That is Hardy-Weinberg.
Exam weight: this is the analytical heart of the chapter, and the only real arithmetic in all of Class 12 Biology.
Lamarck (1809): striving, stretching, inheriting
A giraffe stretches for high leaves. Its neck lengthens a little during its life.
Lamarck claimed: that slightly longer neck is INHERITED, so the next generation starts a little taller.

board_events.text: It is intuitive, almost comforting: effort is rewarded across generations.
The kitchen test: a wrestler trains for years — his newborn is not born muscular.
A woman with pierced ears does not give birth to a baby with pierced ears.
Lamarckism is NOT wrong about everything. Use and disuse DO change the body. It is wrong about ONE thing: those changes are not inherited.
That precision matters — CBSE distinction questions are marked on it.
The experiment that buried Lamarckism
August Weismann cut the tails off mice for 22 successive generations.
Result: not one tail-less mouse was ever born.

board_events.text: Then he explained WHY, with the germplasm theory.
Germplasm = the germ cells (egg and sperm). ONLY these pass to the next generation.
Somatoplasm = the body cells. Changes to them DIE with the individual.
So a cut tail, a trained muscle, a pierced ear — all somatoplasm. There is no route from the body to the next generation.
Pair to memorise: Weismann → germplasm theory → refuted the inheritance of acquired characters.
Darwin (1859): natural selection
Darwin did NOT say organisms strive into new forms.
He said: organisms vary at random; far more are born than can survive.

board_events.caption: Variation, then selection

board_events.text: Those whose variations happen to fit the environment leave more offspring.
Generation after generation, nature quietly 'selects' the better-suited. That is natural selection.
The giraffe's neck lengthened NOT because giraffes tried, but because longer-necked ones ate better and out-reproduced the rest.
The deep switch: for Lamarck the INDIVIDUAL changes. For Darwin the individual does not change — the POPULATION does.
Darwin's two key concepts: branching descent + natural selection. Darwinian fitness = reproductive success, measured by offspring number.
The famous gap, and the two repairs
Darwin's theory had a famous gap: he had no idea HOW variation arose, or HOW it was passed on.
Genetics simply did not exist yet. That is why his theory is 'accepted, but incomplete'.

board_events.caption: de Vries, then the Modern Synthesis
board_events.svg:

<rect x="150" y="40" width="340" height="56" rx="8" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="62" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#d97706">Darwin’s famous gap (1859)</text>
<text x="320" y="82" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">HOW does variation arise? HOW is it passed on? Genetics did not exist yet.</text>
<path d="M240 98 L150 128" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#m1)"/>
<path d="M400 98 L490 128" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#m1)"/>

<text x="163" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Fill 1: de Vries (1901)</text>
<text x="163" y="174" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">SALTATION: evolution by</text>
<text x="163" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">single-step LARGE mutations</text>
<text x="163" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Worked on the evening</text>
<text x="163" y="228" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">primrose, Oenothera</text>
<text x="163" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Mutations: random, directionless</text>
<rect x="332" y="132" width="290" height="128" rx="10" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="477" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">Fill 2: Modern Synthesis (1942)</text>
<text x="477" y="174" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Darwin’s selection MARRIED to</text>
<text x="477" y="190" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Mendelian genetics</text>
<text x="477" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Huxley, Dobzhansky and others</text>
<text x="477" y="234" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Variation: mutation + recombination</text>
<text x="477" y="250" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">Speciation: + reproductive isolation</text>
<rect x="18" y="274" width="604" height="66" rx="10" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="296" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">The one-line distinction CUET loves</text>
<text x="180" y="322" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2563eb">de Vries: mutations are RANDOM & DIRECTIONLESS</text>
<text x="470" y="322" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#d97706">Darwin: variations are SMALL & DIRECTIONAL</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Fill 1 — Hugo de Vries (1901): evolution proceeds by sudden large jumps — mutations, or SALTATION.
From his work on the evening primrose, Oenothera.
Fill 2 — the Modern Synthetic Theory (1942): Darwin's natural selection married to Mendelian genetics. Huxley, Dobzhansky and others.
The modern view: variation arises by mutation and recombination; selection, gene flow and drift change its frequency; reproductive isolation splits populations into species.
The CUET one-liner: de Vries's mutations are 'random and directionless'. Darwin's variations are 'small and directional'.

board_events.text: Proposed by: J.B. Lamarck · C. Darwin & A.R. Wallace · Huxley, Dobzhansky and others.
Engine of change: use & disuse of organs · natural selection of variations · natural selection PLUS genetics.
Source of variation: striving / environmental need · small, random, directional variations · mutation + recombination.
Acquired characters inherited? Lamarck YES — its fatal flaw. Darwin NO. Modern Synthesis NO.
Status: disproved (Weismann) · accepted, but incomplete · currently accepted.
The row that decides most questions is 'acquired characters inherited?'. It is the only row where Lamarck stands alone.
Learn it row by row, not column by column. Every exam item attacks one row.
Five terms, five one-line answers
Inheritance of acquired characters: Lamarck's claim that body changes gained during life pass to offspring. Refuted by Weismann's germplasm theory.
Natural selection: differential survival and reproduction of individuals carrying favourable HERITABLE variations.

board_events.text: Darwinian fitness: an individual's reproductive success — measured by the NUMBER OF OFFSPRING left, not by strength or size.
Saltation (de Vries): evolution by single-step large mutations. Based on his work on the evening primrose, Oenothera.
Neo-Darwinism / Modern Synthesis: Darwin's selection updated with genetics, molecular biology, palaeontology and ecology. Speciation = genetic variation + selection + reproductive isolation.
Darwin's two key concepts, asked directly: branching descent AND natural selection.
CUET favours one-line distinctions. These are the one-liners.

segments.text: We close this part with the single most useful thing in the subtopic, and it takes three seconds to run.
Ask only one question. Is the underlying structure the same? That is it. That is the whole method. Do not read the options. Do not think about what the organs do. One question.
Look at the board. One question at the top, two branches, and everything below each branch is automatic once you have answered it.
If yes, the structure is the same, then: homologous, divergent, common ancestry. Three words that arrive together, every time, in that order.
And here is the part that takes discipline. Regardless of what the organs do. A thorn and a tendril do opposite jobs and are still homologous. Function does not get a vote.
If no, the structure is different, but the function matches, then: analogous, convergent. Again three words arriving together.
And the meaning: similar environment, not ancestry. The environment pushed two unrelated things towards the same solution.

<whisper> So here is why this works. Function is the distractor. It is loud, it is the first thing you notice, and it is deliberately what the question waves in front of you. Structure is the deciding clue, and it is quiet.
One question. Every homology and analogy item in this chapter falls to it. That is where we will stop for this part.
Every theory of evolution in this chapter is really an attempt to answer one stubborn question, and if you hold that question in your head, the whole subtopic organises itself around it.
The question is this. Life clearly changes over time. Nobody serious disputes that any more. But what is the engine driving the change?
Three big answers were offered, one after another. And here is why we study all three rather than just the winner: watching them rise and fall is the best way to understand evolution itself.
Look at the board. Three boxes, left to right, and a verdict stamped under each one.
First, Lamarck, in eighteen oh nine. Organisms strive, and what they practise during life gets passed to their children. Verdict: disproved.

Second, Darwin, in eighteen fifty-nine. Organisms vary at random, and nature quietly selects the better-suited. Verdict: accepted, but incomplete. Hold on to that second word, because the incompleteness is what drives the rest of the story.
Third, the Modern Synthesis, in nineteen forty-two. Darwin's selection married to genetics. Verdict: currently accepted.

<curious> And then, at the bottom of the board, something clever happens. We flip the question over. Instead of asking what makes a population evolve, we ask what a population would look like if it were not evolving at all. That hypothetical, do-nothing population is exactly what the Hardy-Weinberg principle describes.

Take this subtopic seriously. It is the analytical heart of the chapter, a guaranteed scorer, and the Hardy-Weinberg equation is the only real arithmetic in all of Class twelve Biology. Practise it until it is automatic.
The first answer came from Lamarck, and I want you to feel why it convinced people.
Take the giraffe. It stretches for high leaves, day after day, and over its lifetime its neck does lengthen a little. That much is true: bodies respond to use.
Then Lamarck took one more step. He claimed that slightly longer neck is inherited, so the next generation starts taller, stretches from there, and compounds.
Follow the board left to right. Generation one stretches. The neck lengthens in life. Generation two, in red, supposedly starts taller. The theory lives or dies on that red arrow.
And notice how appealing this is. It is intuitive, almost comforting: effort is rewarded across generations. A lovely idea, which is exactly why it needed killing carefully.
So here is the kitchen test, and you can run it without a laboratory. A wrestler builds huge muscles through years of training. His newborn is not born muscular.
A woman with pierced ears does not give birth to a baby with pierced ears. What happens to the body during life does not travel to the next generation.

<curious> But now the precision that earns marks. Lamarckism is not wrong about everything. Use and disuse really do change the body. It is wrong about exactly one thing: those changes are not inherited.

So look at the panel on the right. Idea one, green, true. Idea two, red, false. When a distinction question compares Lamarck and Darwin, that split is what you are marked on. Do not write that Lamarck was simply wrong. Write which half was wrong.
The kitchen test is persuasive, but it is anecdote. August Weismann turned it into an experiment, and then into an explanation.
He cut the tails off mice, bred them, cut the tails off their offspring, and bred those. He kept going for twenty-two successive generations.
The result: not one tail-less mouse was ever born. Not one, across twenty-two generations. If acquired characters were inherited, something should have budged. Nothing did.
Look at the board. The top strip is the experiment, running left to right until it hits that red box. The bottom half is the part that actually matters.
An experiment that only says no is half a result. Weismann explained why the answer had to be no, with his germplasm theory.
Germplasm means the germ cells: egg and sperm. Only these pass to the next generation. They are the only bridge across the gap between one generation and the next.
Somatoplasm means the body cells. Everything else. Muscle, skin, bone, tail. And changes to them die with the individual, because they are not on the bridge.

<excited> Now put the two together and watch Lamarckism collapse. A cut tail is somatoplasm. A trained muscle is somatoplasm. A pierced ear is somatoplasm. There is no route from the body to the next generation. Not a weak route. No route at all.

One pair to memorise cold, because it is a standing C U E T item. Weismann goes with the germplasm theory, and the germplasm theory refuted the inheritance of acquired characters. Not natural selection. Not drift. The inheritance of acquired characters.
The second answer was Darwin's, and it is the one that survived. But it is easy to hear Darwin and quietly translate him back into Lamarck, so listen closely.
Darwin did not say organisms strive into new forms. Delete striving from the story entirely. Nobody is trying, nobody is reaching, nobody wants anything.
What he said is this. Organisms vary at random. And far more are born than can possibly survive.
Look at the left panel. Three giraffes, necks already different, and nobody earned it. The variation is just there, before any environment gets a vote.
Now the environment votes. Those whose variations happen to fit leave more offspring. Notice the word happen. It is luck about what you were born with, not merit.
And repeat that, generation after generation, and nature quietly selects the better-suited without intending anything. That is natural selection. It is a filter, not a designer.
So run the giraffe again, Darwin's way. The neck lengthened not because giraffes tried, but because among naturally varying necks, the longer-necked ones ate better and out-reproduced the rest.

<excited> And here is the deep switch, on the right of the board. For Lamarck, the individual changes and passes the change on. For Darwin, the individual does not change at all. The population does. That single sentence is the difference between the two theories.

Two more things to carry. Darwin's two key concepts are branching descent and natural selection. And Darwinian fitness is reproductive success, measured by offspring number, not strength or size. The strongest animal that leaves no offspring has a fitness of zero.
Darwin's theory survived, but it had a famous gap, and that gap is examinable in its own right.
The gap is this. He had no idea how variation arose, or how it was passed on. He built an entire engine around variation without being able to say where it comes from.
And that is not a criticism of him. Genetics did not exist yet; Mendel's work sat unread. So when the table says Darwin is accepted but incomplete, this gap is the incompleteness.
Look at the board. The amber box at the top is the gap, and two arrows come down out of it, because the gap was filled twice.
Fill one, Hugo de Vries, nineteen oh one. Evolution proceeds by sudden large jumps, which he called mutations. The process has a name you must know: saltation, from the Latin for a leap.
And the organism attached to it is the evening primrose, Oenothera. De Vries, primrose, saltation. That trio travels together.
Fill two, and this is the one that stuck: the Modern Synthetic Theory, nineteen forty-two. Darwin's natural selection married to Mendelian genetics. The names are Huxley, Dobzhansky and others.

So here is the modern view in one breath. Variation arises by mutation and recombination. Natural selection, gene flow and genetic drift change its frequency. And reproductive isolation splits populations into species.

<whisper> Now the line C U E T asks about, in the red box. De Vries called his mutations random and directionless. Darwin called his variations small and directional. The exam quotes those two phrases almost word for word.
We have met all three theories separately. Now put them side by side, because N E E T asks this as a table and C B S E as a two-mark distinction.
Look at the board. Five rows, three columns. And learn it row by row, not column by column, because that is how it is examined.
Row one, proposed by. Lamarck, alone. Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, and Wallace gets dropped constantly. The Modern Synthesis: Huxley, Dobzhansky and others.
Row two, engine of change. Use and disuse of organs. Natural selection of variations. Natural selection plus genetics. The third is not a new engine; it is the second with a fuel supply attached.
Row three, source of variation. Lamarck: striving, or environmental need. Darwin: small, random, directional variations. Modern Synthesis: mutation and recombination. This row is where the gap lives.

<excited> Row four, and this row decides most questions. Are acquired characters inherited? Lamarck: yes, its fatal flaw. Darwin: no. Modern Synthesis: no. Look at the shape. It is the only row where Lamarck stands completely alone.
Row five, status. Disproved, by Weismann. Accepted, but incomplete. Currently accepted. Three verdicts, each a one-word answer to a possible question.

So use the shape. If an item is about inheritance of acquired characters, the answer is always Lamarck, because nobody else claims it. If it is about the source of variation, you choose between striving, small random variations, and mutation plus recombination.
One instruction before you memorise this: read every row across before you read any column down. Rows are the unit of memory here.
C U E T favours one-line distinctions here, so here are the one-liners. Five terms, and hear the precise wording, because the precision is the mark.

Inheritance of acquired characters. Lamarck's claim that body changes gained during life pass to offspring. Refuted by Weismann's germplasm theory. The definition contains its own refutation. Never state this term without naming Weismann.
Natural selection. Differential survival and reproduction of individuals carrying favourable heritable variations. And listen to the word heritable, because that is the word doing all the work.
Look at the cards on the board. The word heritable is what separates Darwin's box from Lamarck's box, and it is exactly the word students drop.

Darwinian fitness. An individual's reproductive success, measured by the number of offspring left. Not strength. Not size. Not lifespan. The most misunderstood term in the chapter, because everyday English means something else by fit.
Saltation, from de Vries. Evolution by single-step large mutations. Based on his work on the evening primrose, Oenothera. One word, one scientist, one plant.

Neo-Darwinism, also called the Modern Synthesis. Darwin's selection updated with genetics, molecular biology, palaeontology and ecology. And its account of speciation: genetic variation, plus selection, plus reproductive isolation.

<curious> And the one at the bottom of the board, asked directly and often. Darwin's two key concepts. Branching descent and natural selection. Two, and both are named. Students reliably remember the second and forget the first.
So drill these as sentences. If a C U E T item gives a definition and asks for the name, the wording will be close to what I just read.
इस part को हम subtopic की सबसे काम की चीज़ से बंद करते हैं, और इसे चलाने में तीन सेकंड लगते हैं।
सिर्फ़ एक सवाल पूछिए। क्या underlying structure एक जैसा है? बस। यही पूरा method है। Options मत पढ़िए। ये मत सोचिए कि organs करते क्या हैं। एक सवाल।
Board देखिए। ऊपर एक सवाल, दो शाखाएँ, और जवाब देते ही हर शाखा के नीचे सब कुछ अपने आप हो जाता है।
अगर हाँ, structure एक जैसा है, तो: homologous, divergent, common ancestry. तीन शब्द जो हर बार साथ आते हैं, इसी क्रम में।
और यहीं अनुशासन चाहिए। चाहे organs कुछ भी करते हों। एक thorn और एक tendril उल्टे काम करते हैं और फिर भी homologous हैं। Function को वोट का हक़ नहीं है।
अगर नहीं, structure अलग है, लेकिन function मिलता है, तो: analogous, convergent. फिर तीन शब्द, साथ-साथ।
और इसका मतलब: एक जैसा environment, ancestry नहीं। Environment ने दो असंबंधित चीज़ों को एक ही हल की तरफ़ धकेल दिया।
<whisper> तो ये काम क्यों करता है, समझिए। Function distractor है। वो शोर मचाता है, सबसे पहले वही दिखता है, और सवाल जानबूझकर उसी को आपके सामने लहराता है। Structure निर्णायक clue है, और वो चुप रहता है।
एक सवाल। इस chapter का हर homology-analogy item इसके आगे गिर जाता है। इस part के लिए हम यहीं रुकेंगे।
इस chapter की हर theory of evolution असल में एक ही ज़िद्दी सवाल का जवाब देने की कोशिश है, और अगर वो सवाल आपके दिमाग़ में बैठ जाए, तो पूरा subtopic अपने आप उसी के इर्द-गिर्द सज जाता है।
सवाल ये है। Life समय के साथ बदलती है — इससे अब कोई गंभीर आदमी इनकार नहीं करता। लेकिन इस बदलाव का engine क्या है?
तीन बड़े जवाब आए, एक के बाद एक। और हम सिर्फ़ जीतने वाले को नहीं, तीनों को क्यों पढ़ते हैं — ये समझिए। इनका उठना और गिरना देखना ही evolution को समझने का सबसे अच्छा तरीक़ा है।
Board देखिए। तीन boxes, बाएँ से दाएँ, और हर एक के नीचे ठप्पा लगा फ़ैसला।
पहला, Lamarck, अठारह सौ नौ में। जीव कोशिश करते हैं, और जो वो ज़िंदगी में अभ्यास करते हैं वो उनके बच्चों तक पहुँच जाता है। फ़ैसला: disproved.

दूसरा, Darwin, अठारह सौ उनसठ में। जीवों में random variation होता है, और nature चुपचाप बेहतर फ़िट होने वालों को select कर लेती है। फ़ैसला: accepted, लेकिन incomplete. इस दूसरे शब्द को पकड़ लीजिए, क्योंकि यही अधूरापन आगे की पूरी कहानी चलाता है।
तीसरा, Modern Synthesis, उन्नीस सौ बयालीस में। Darwin का selection, genetics से ब्याह दिया गया। फ़ैसला: फ़िलहाल accepted.

<curious> और फिर board के नीचे एक होशियारी होती है। हम सवाल को उल्टा पलट देते हैं। ये पूछने के बजाय कि population को evolve क्या कराता है, हम पूछते हैं कि अगर population evolve कर ही न रही हो तो वो कैसी दिखेगी। वही काल्पनिक, कुछ-न-करने वाली population ही Hardy-Weinberg principle है।

इस subtopic को गंभीरता से लीजिए। ये chapter का analytical दिल है, ये पक्का scorer है, और Hardy-Weinberg equation पूरी Class बारह Biology की इकलौती असली arithmetic है। इसे तब तक practise कीजिए जब तक ये automatic न हो जाए।
पहला जवाब Lamarck से आया, और मैं चाहता हूँ आप महसूस करें कि इसने लोगों को क्यों समझा लिया, क्योंकि आपको ऐसे students मिलेंगे जो आज भी इसे मानते हैं।
Giraffe को लीजिए। वो ऊँची पत्तियों के लिए दिन-ब-दिन गर्दन तानती है, और उसकी ज़िंदगी में गर्दन थोड़ी लंबी हो भी जाती है। यहाँ तक बात सच है। शरीर इस्तेमाल का जवाब देता है।
फिर Lamarck ने एक क़दम और बढ़ाया। उन्होंने कहा कि वो थोड़ी लंबी गर्दन inherit होती है, तो अगली पीढ़ी थोड़ी ऊँची शुरू करती है, वहाँ से और तानती है, और ये सिलसिला बढ़ता जाता है।
Board को बाएँ से दाएँ follow कीजिए। पहली generation तानती है। ज़िंदगी में गर्दन लंबी होती है। दूसरी generation, लाल रंग में, कथित तौर पर ऊँची शुरू करती है। पूरी theory उसी लाल तीर पर जीती या मरती है।

और देखिए ये कितना लुभावना है। ये सहज है, लगभग दिलासा देने वाला। मेहनत का फल पीढ़ियों तक जाता है। जिसके लिए आप मेहनत करें, वो आपके बच्चों को मिले। बहुत प्यारा idea है — इसीलिए इसे बड़े ध्यान से मारना पड़ा।
तो ये रहा kitchen test, जिसे आप बिना laboratory के चला सकते हैं। एक wrestler सालों की training से भारी muscles बनाता है। उसका नवजात muscular पैदा नहीं होता।
जिस औरत के कान छिदे हों, उसका बच्चा छिदे कानों के साथ पैदा नहीं होता। ज़िंदगी में शरीर के साथ जो होता है, वो अगली पीढ़ी तक जाता ही नहीं।

<curious> लेकिन अब वो बारीकी जो marks दिलाती है, और ज़्यादातर students यहाँ उल्टी दिशा में ग़लत होते हैं। Lamarckism हर बात में ग़लत नहीं है। Use और disuse सचमुच शरीर बदलते हैं। ये सिर्फ़ एक बात में ग़लत है: वो बदलाव inherit नहीं होते।

तो board के दाएँ panel को देखिए। Idea एक, हरा, सही। Idea दो, लाल, ग़लत। जब कोई distinction सवाल Lamarck और Darwin की तुलना माँगे, तो आपको इसी बँटवारे पर marks मिलते हैं। ये मत लिखिए कि Lamarck बस ग़लत थे। ये लिखिए कि कौन सा आधा ग़लत था।
Kitchen test असरदार है, लेकिन वो क़िस्सा है। August Weismann ने उसे experiment बनाया, और फिर — जो ज़्यादा अहम है — एक व्याख्या बनाया।
उन्होंने चूहों की पूँछें काट दीं। फिर उनकी breeding की, उनके बच्चों की पूँछें काटीं, और उनकी breeding की। ये सिलसिला बाईस लगातार पीढ़ियों तक चला।
नतीजा: एक भी बिना पूँछ का चूहा कभी पैदा नहीं हुआ। एक भी नहीं, बाईस पीढ़ियों की लगातार पूँछ-कटाई के बावजूद। अगर acquired characters inherit होते, तो कुछ तो हिलता। कुछ नहीं हिला।
Board देखिए। ऊपर की पट्टी experiment है, जो बाएँ से दाएँ चलकर उस लाल box से टकराती है। असली बात नीचे का आधा हिस्सा है।
क्योंकि जो experiment सिर्फ़ ना कहे, वो आधा नतीजा है। Weismann आगे गए और बताया कि जवाब ना क्यों होना ही था — अपनी germplasm theory से।
Germplasm यानी germ cells: egg और sperm. और उनका दावा है कि सिर्फ़ यही अगली पीढ़ी तक जाते हैं। एक पीढ़ी से दूसरी तक की खाई पर यही इकलौता पुल हैं।
Somatoplasm यानी body cells. बाक़ी सब कुछ। Muscle, skin, bone, पूँछ। और उनके बदलाव उस individual के साथ ही मर जाते हैं, क्योंकि वो पुल पर हैं ही नहीं।

<excited> अब दोनों को जोड़िए और पूरे Lamarckism को ढहते देखिए। कटी पूँछ somatoplasm है। Training से बना muscle somatoplasm है। छिदा कान somatoplasm है। शरीर से अगली पीढ़ी तक कोई रास्ता है ही नहीं। कमज़ोर रास्ता नहीं — कोई रास्ता नहीं।

एक जोड़ा पक्का याद कीजिए, क्योंकि ये C U E T का जमा हुआ item है। Weismann का जोड़ है germplasm theory, और germplasm theory ने inheritance of acquired characters को refute किया। Natural selection को नहीं। Drift को नहीं। Inheritance of acquired characters को।
दूसरा जवाब Darwin का था, और यही बचा। लेकिन Darwin को सुनकर चुपचाप उसे वापस Lamarck में अनुवाद कर देना आसान है, तो फ़र्क़ पर कान लगाइए।
Darwin ने ये नहीं कहा कि जीव कोशिश करके नए रूप बन जाते हैं। कहानी से striving को पूरी तरह हटा दीजिए। कोई कोशिश नहीं कर रहा, कोई तान नहीं रहा, किसी को कुछ चाहिए नहीं।
उन्होंने ये कहा। जीवों में random variation होता है। और जितने बच सकते हैं, उससे कहीं ज़्यादा पैदा होते हैं।
बायाँ panel देखिए। तीन giraffes, गर्दनें पहले से अलग, और किसी ने इसे कमाने के लिए कुछ नहीं किया। Variation बस मौजूद है, इससे पहले कि environment को वोट मिले।

अब environment वोट डालता है। जिनका variation इत्तेफ़ाक़ से फ़िट बैठता है, वो ज़्यादा बच्चे छोड़ते हैं। इत्तेफ़ाक़ शब्द पर ध्यान दीजिए। ये क़िस्मत की बात है कि आप कौन सा variation लेकर पैदा हुए, मेहनत की नहीं।
और इसे पीढ़ी-दर-पीढ़ी दोहराइए, तो nature बिना कोई इरादा रखे चुपचाप बेहतर फ़िट को select कर लेती है। यही natural selection है। ये filter है, designer नहीं।

तो giraffe को दोबारा चलाइए, Darwin के तरीक़े से। गर्दन इसलिए लंबी नहीं हुई कि giraffes ने कोशिश की, बल्कि इसलिए कि क़ुदरती तौर पर अलग-अलग गर्दनों वाली population में लंबी गर्दन वालों ने बेहतर खाया और बाक़ियों से ज़्यादा बच्चे छोड़े।

<excited> और अब वो गहरा फ़र्क़, board के दाईं तरफ़। Lamarck के लिए individual बदलता है और बदलाव आगे भेजता है। Darwin के लिए individual बदलता ही नहीं। Population बदलती है। यही एक वाक्य दोनों theories का फ़र्क़ है।

दो और चीज़ें साथ ले जाइए। Darwin के दो key concepts हैं branching descent और natural selection. और Darwinian fitness मतलब reproductive success, जो छोड़े गए बच्चों की संख्या से नापी जाती है, ताक़त या size से नहीं। जो सबसे ताक़तवर जानवर कोई बच्चा नहीं छोड़ता, उसकी fitness शून्य है।
Darwin की theory बच गई, लेकिन उसमें एक मशहूर gap था, और वो gap ख़ुद examinable है।
Gap ये है। उन्हें पता ही नहीं था कि variation आता कहाँ से है, और न ये कि वो आगे कैसे जाता है। उन्होंने पूरा engine variation के इर्द-गिर्द बना दिया, बिना ये बता पाए कि variation कहाँ से आता है।
और ये उन पर इल्ज़ाम नहीं है। Genetics तब मौजूद ही नहीं थी। Mendel का काम बिना पढ़े रखा था। तो जब table कहती है कि Darwin accepted लेकिन incomplete हैं, तो यही gap वो अधूरापन है।
Board देखिए। ऊपर का amber box वही gap है, और उसमें से दो तीर नीचे आते हैं, क्योंकि ये gap दो बार भरा गया।

पहली भराई, Hugo de Vries, उन्नीस सौ एक में। उन्होंने कहा कि evolution अचानक बड़ी छलांगों से चलता है, जिन्हें उन्होंने mutations कहा। इस process का नाम आपको आना चाहिए: saltation, जो छलांग के Latin शब्द से बना है।
और इससे जुड़ा जीव है evening primrose, यानी Oenothera. De Vries, primrose, saltation. ये तिकड़ी साथ चलती है।
दूसरी भराई, और यही टिकी: Modern Synthetic Theory, उन्नीस सौ बयालीस। Darwin के natural selection का Mendelian genetics से ब्याह। नाम हैं Huxley, Dobzhansky और दूसरे।

तो एक साँस में आधुनिक नज़रिया ये है। Variation mutation और recombination से आता है। Natural selection, gene flow और genetic drift उसकी frequency बदलते हैं। और reproductive isolation populations को species में बाँट देता है।

<whisper> अब वो line जो C U E T पूछता है, नीचे के लाल box में। De Vries ने अपने mutations को random और directionless कहा। Darwin ने अपने variations को small और directional कहा। यही दोनों phrases वो distinction हैं, और exam इन्हें लगभग शब्द-दर-शब्द quote करता है।
तीनों theories हम अलग-अलग देख चुके हैं। अब इन्हें साथ रखिए, क्योंकि N E E T इसे table की तरह पूछता है और C B S E दो-mark वाली distinction की तरह।
Board देखिए। पाँच rows, तीन columns. और इसे row by row सीखिए, column by column नहीं, क्योंकि इसकी परीक्षा ऐसे ही होती है।

Row एक, proposed by. Lamarckism में अकेले J. B. Lamarck. Darwinism में Charles Darwin और Alfred Russel Wallace — और Wallace को students लगातार गिरा देते हैं। Modern Synthesis में Huxley, Dobzhansky और दूसरे।

Row दो, engine of change. Use और disuse of organs. Variations का natural selection. Natural selection साथ में genetics. ध्यान दीजिए तीसरा कोई नया engine नहीं है, वो दूसरा engine ही है जिसमें ईंधन की सप्लाई जोड़ दी गई।

Row तीन, source of variation. Lamarck: striving, या environmental need. Darwin: small, random, directional variations. Modern Synthesis: mutation और recombination. इसी row में gap की पूरी कहानी रहती है।

<excited> Row चार, और यही row ज़्यादातर सवाल तय करती है। क्या acquired characters inherit होते हैं? Lamarck: हाँ, और यही उसकी fatal flaw है। Darwin: नहीं। Modern Synthesis: नहीं। इस row का आकार देखिए। यही इकलौती row है जहाँ Lamarck बिल्कुल अकेला खड़ा है।
Row पाँच, status. Disproved, Weismann द्वारा। Accepted, लेकिन incomplete. फ़िलहाल accepted. तीन अलग फ़ैसले, और हर एक किसी संभावित सवाल का एक-शब्द का जवाब है।

तो इस आकार का इस्तेमाल कीजिए। अगर item inheritance of acquired characters पर है, तो जवाब हमेशा Lamarck है, क्योंकि ये दावा और कोई करता ही नहीं। अगर source of variation पर है, तो आप striving, small random variations, और mutation plus recombination में से चुन रहे हैं।
याद करने से पहले एक पढ़ने का निर्देश। कोई भी column नीचे पढ़ने से पहले हर row को आर-पार पढ़िए। हर exam item एक row पर हमला करता है, तो यहाँ याद्दाश्त की इकाई row है।
इस subtopic में C U E T को one-line distinctions पसंद हैं, तो ये रहे one-liners. पाँच terms, और मैं चाहता हूँ आप सटीक शब्द सुनें, क्योंकि सटीकता ही mark है।

Inheritance of acquired characters. Lamarck का दावा कि ज़िंदगी में शरीर में आए बदलाव बच्चों तक जाते हैं। Weismann की germplasm theory ने इसे refute किया। ध्यान दीजिए definition में ही उसका खंडन शामिल है। ये जानबूझकर है। इस term को कभी Weismann का नाम लिए बिना मत लिखिए।
Natural selection. Favourable heritable variations वाले individuals का differential survival और reproduction. और heritable शब्द को ग़ौर से सुनिए, क्योंकि सारा काम वही कर रहा है।
Board पर cards देखिए। Heritable शब्द ही Darwin के box को Lamarck के box से अलग करता है, और ठीक यही शब्द students गिरा देते हैं।

Darwinian fitness. किसी individual की reproductive success, जो छोड़े गए बच्चों की संख्या से नापी जाती है। ताक़त से नहीं। Size से नहीं। कितना जिया, इससे नहीं। ये chapter का सबसे ज़्यादा ग़लत समझा जाने वाला term है, क्योंकि रोज़मर्रा की English में fit का मतलब कुछ और है।
Saltation, de Vries से। Single-step बड़े mutations से evolution. उनके evening primrose, Oenothera पर काम पर आधारित। एक शब्द, एक scientist, एक पौधा।

Neo-Darwinism, जिसे Modern Synthesis भी कहते हैं। Darwin का selection, genetics, molecular biology, palaeontology और ecology से update किया हुआ। और speciation की इसकी व्याख्या: genetic variation, साथ selection, साथ reproductive isolation.

<curious> और board के नीचे वाला, जो सीधे और अक्सर पूछा जाता है। Darwin के दो key concepts. Branching descent और natural selection. दो, और दोनों नाम लेकर। Students दूसरा पक्का याद रखते हैं और पहला भूल जाते हैं।
तो इन्हें वाक्यों की तरह रटिए, एहसास की तरह नहीं। अगर C U E T item आपको definition देकर नाम पूछे, तो शब्द लगभग वही होंगे जो मैंने अभी पढ़े।

board_events.text: STABILISING: favours the average; removes both extremes. The peak gets taller and narrower.
Example: human birth weight clustering near a mean.
DIRECTIONAL: favours ONE extreme. The peak shifts toward that extreme.
Example: darker peppered moths in soot-darkened cities.
DISRUPTIVE: favours BOTH extremes; removes the average. The curve splits into two peaks.
Example: bill sizes splitting where only large and small seeds exist. Read the CURVE, not the story: one peak taller, one peak moved, or two peaks.
Hardy-Weinberg describes a population that is NOT evolving
Stop asking 'what makes a population evolve?'. Ask instead: 'what would it look like if it were NOT evolving at all?'

board_events.text: Physics: Newton's first law — an object keeps its velocity unless a force acts.
Biology: Hardy-Weinberg — allele frequencies stay constant unless an evolutionary force acts.
The principle's real job is NOT to describe reality. Almost no real population is in perfect equilibrium.
Its job is to give a yardstick against which evolution becomes VISIBLE.
Frequencies match the prediction → nothing is pushing the population.
Frequencies drift from the prediction → some evolutionary force is at work, and the SIZE of the gap measures how much.
Four terms, and the distinction that decides every numerical
Gene pool: ALL the alleles of ALL genes in a population.

board_events.caption: The two lines you must never mix
board_events.svg:

<text x="32" y="64" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Gene pool</text>
<text x="32" y="84" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">ALL the alleles of ALL the genes in a population.</text>

<text x="163" y="207" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">q = frequency of recessive a</text>
<rect x="46" y="218" width="234" height="24" rx="5" fill="#d97706"/>
<text x="163" y="235" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">p + q = 1</text>
<rect x="332" y="122" width="290" height="126" rx="10" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="477" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">GENOTYPE frequencies</text>
<rect x="360" y="152" width="234" height="24" rx="5" fill="#d1fae5"/>
<text x="477" y="169" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">AA = p²   (homozygous dominant)</text>
<rect x="360" y="180" width="234" height="24" rx="5" fill="#d1fae5"/>
<text x="477" y="197" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">Aa = 2pq  (heterozygous)</text>
<rect x="360" y="208" width="234" height="24" rx="5" fill="#d1fae5"/>
<text x="477" y="225" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">aa = q²   (homozygous recessive)</text>
<rect x="360" y="236" width="234" height="6" fill="#059669"/>
<rect x="18" y="260" width="604" height="36" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="284" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Mixing these two lines is the commonest numerical error in the chapter</text>
<rect x="18" y="304" width="604" height="40" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="32" y="320" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Genetic (Hardy–Weinberg) equilibrium:</text>
<text x="32" y="336" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">the state in which allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Allele frequency: $p$ = frequency of the dominant allele A; $q$ = frequency of the recessive allele a. With two alleles, $p + q = 1$.
Genotype frequencies: $p^2$ = AA (homozygous dominant); $2pq$ = Aa (heterozygous); $q^2$ = aa (homozygous recessive).
Mixing allele frequencies with genotype frequencies is the COMMONEST numerical error in the chapter.
Genetic (Hardy-Weinberg) equilibrium: the state in which allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation.
Frequencies are dimensionless and must sum to one. There are no SI units here.
The only sanity checks you need: $p + q = 1$ and $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$.
Equilibrium holds only when ALL five are true
Each condition is simply 'switch OFF one evolutionary force'.

<text x="96" y="160" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Random mating</text>
<text x="96" y="176" font-size="11" fill="#475569">no mate choice based on genotype</text>
<rect x="40" y="190" width="560" height="42" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="68" cy="211" r="13" fill="#059669"/><text x="68" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">3</text>
<text x="96" y="208" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">No mutation</text>
<text x="96" y="224" font-size="11" fill="#475569">no new alleles created or converted</text>
<rect x="40" y="238" width="560" height="42" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="68" cy="259" r="13" fill="#059669"/><text x="68" y="264" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">4</text>
<text x="96" y="256" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">No gene flow (migration)</text>
<text x="96" y="272" font-size="11" fill="#475569">no alleles entering or leaving</text>
<rect x="40" y="286" width="560" height="42" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="68" cy="307" r="13" fill="#059669"/><text x="68" y="312" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">5</text>
<text x="96" y="304" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">No natural selection</text>
<text x="96" y="320" font-size="11" fill="#475569">no genotype out-reproduces another</text>

board_events.text: 1. Large population — so chance fluctuations (genetic drift) are negligible.
2. Random mating — no mate choice based on genotype.
3. No mutation — no new alleles created or converted.
4. No gene flow (migration) — no alleles entering or leaving.
5. No natural selection — no genotype out-reproduces another.
Break any ONE and the population evolves. Real populations rarely satisfy all five — which is exactly WHY evolution happens.
Break a condition, and you get a FORCE
These are the mirror image of the conditions. These five ARE evolution.

board_events.caption: The five disturbing factors

<text x="52" y="236" font-size="10" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Bottleneck effect</text>
<text x="52" y="249" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">a crash leaves survivors with shifted frequencies</text>
<rect x="332" y="84" width="290" height="46" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="346" y="104" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#d97706">3. Mutation</text>
<text x="346" y="122" font-size="10" fill="#475569">slow, random; the ULTIMATE origin of all variation</text>
<rect x="332" y="138" width="290" height="46" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="346" y="158" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#d97706">4. Genetic recombination</text>
<text x="346" y="176" font-size="10" fill="#475569">crossing over at meiosis shuffles alleles into new combinations</text>
<rect x="332" y="192" width="290" height="66" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="346" y="212" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">5. Natural selection</text>
<text x="346" y="230" font-size="10" fill="#475569">non-random survival and reproduction</text>
<text x="346" y="248" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">the MAIN directional force</text>
<rect x="18" y="268" width="604" height="72" rx="10" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/>

</svg>

board_events.text: 1. Gene migration / gene flow — alleles added to or lost from a population shift its frequencies. Repeated migration makes this a steady force.
2. Genetic drift — random change in allele frequency by chance; powerful in SMALL populations.

Two special cases of drift. Founder effect: a few individuals start a new population carrying only a slice of the original gene pool. Bottleneck effect: a population crash leaves survivors whose allele frequencies differ from the original.
3. Mutation — slow, random source of brand-new alleles; the ultimate origin of ALL variation.
4. Genetic recombination — crossing over during meiosis shuffles alleles into new combinations.
5. Natural selection — non-random survival and reproduction; the MAIN directional force. Memory aid: 'Genes Drift, Mutate, Recombine, get Selected'.
How the baseline turns into a measuring instrument
Predicted: the $p^2 : 2pq : q^2$ ratio — what a NON-evolving population must show.

board_events.text: Measured: the counts you actually find in the field.
No gap → no force is acting; the population is in equilibrium.
Gap → one of the five forces is acting, and the SIZE of the gap measures how much. That is how Hardy-Weinberg becomes a detector of evolution.
Precision note: mutation and recombination mainly SUPPLY variation. Strictly, recombination reshuffles existing alleles and does not by itself change allele frequencies.
NCERT lists all five as factors affecting equilibrium — that is the exam-expected answer.
But selection and drift are the forces that actually push frequencies in a direction. Know both the exam answer and the truth behind it.
Two alleles: A with frequency $p$, a with frequency $q$
Step 1 — gametes carry alleles in the same proportion. Each gamete carries ONE allele, so the fraction of sperm carrying A is $p$ and carrying a is $q$. The same is true of eggs.
Why it matters: it lets us treat fertilisation as drawing one allele from the 'sperm pool' and one from the 'egg pool'.

segments.text: Selection is not one thing. It comes in three flavours, and the exam asks you to tell them apart from a description or a graph. Learn them as shapes.
Set up the picture. Plot number of individuals up the vertical axis against phenotype along the horizontal. You get a bell curve. Selection changes its shape, and each type changes it differently.
Look at the three panels. Dashed curve is before. Solid curve is after. Shaded regions are what selection removed.
Panel one, stabilising selection. It favours the average and removes both extremes, so the peak gets taller and narrower. Nothing moves sideways. The population just becomes more alike.
The example to quote is human birth weight clustering near a mean. Very small and very large babies both fared badly, so the middle wins from both sides.
Panel two, directional selection. It favours one extreme, so the whole peak shifts toward that extreme. Watch the arrow. The curve does not get narrower, it walks.
The example is darker peppered moths in soot-darkened cities. Soot made pale moths visible to predators, so the population marched toward dark. One direction, one shift.
Panel three, disruptive selection. It favours both extremes and removes the average, so the curve splits into two peaks. This is the only one that turns one population into two shapes.

<curious> The example is bill sizes splitting where only large and small seeds exist. No medium seeds, so no living for a medium bill. And the technique for all three: read the curve, not the story. One peak taller, one peak moved, or two peaks. That is the diagnosis.
Now we flip the question, and this flip is the most important move in the subtopic. Get it and the numericals become obvious. Miss it and Hardy-Weinberg feels like arbitrary algebra.

Stop asking what makes a population evolve. Ask instead: what would a population look like if it were not evolving at all? That hypothetical, do-nothing population is exactly what the Hardy-Weinberg principle describes.
Look at the board, because the analogy on it is worth more than the equation right now.
On the left, physics. Newton's first law. An object keeps its velocity unless a force acts on it. Nobody complains that this is unrealistic, even though friction is everywhere.
On the right, biology. Hardy-Weinberg. Allele frequencies stay constant unless an evolutionary force acts. Same structure. Same job. A statement of what happens when nothing happens.

So here is the point students find genuinely strange. The principle's real job is not to describe reality. Almost no real population is in perfect equilibrium. Hardy-Weinberg is not trying to be true of the world.
Its job is to be a yardstick. Once you have a picture of a population going nowhere, evolution becomes visible as a departure from it. You cannot see motion without something to be still against.
So the reading rule, at the bottom of the board. If a real population's allele frequencies match the Hardy-Weinberg prediction, nothing is pushing it.

<curious> And if they drift away from the prediction, some evolutionary force is at work, and the size of the gap measures how much. That is not a side remark. That is what the whole principle is for.
Four terms, and one distinction inside them that decides whether your numericals come out right.

Gene pool. All the alleles of all the genes in a population. Not one organism's alleles. The whole population's shared stock. That is what Hardy-Weinberg is about, and why it refuses to talk about individuals.
Now look at the two panels — the two lines you must never mix.

Left panel, allele frequencies. P is the frequency of the dominant allele, capital A. Q is the frequency of the recessive allele, small a. With two alleles, p plus q equals one. Two things, two frequencies, accounting for everything.
Right panel, genotype frequencies. P squared is A A. Two p q is A a. Q squared is a a. Three things now, because two alleles make three genotypes.

<excited> And here is the sentence to write on your wall. Mixing allele frequencies with genotype frequencies is the commonest numerical error in the chapter. Not a rare slip. The commonest one. The examiner knows it, and the distractors are built out of it.

One more term. Genetic equilibrium, also called Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium: the state in which allele frequencies stay constant from generation to generation. Notice it is defined on alleles, not genotypes.
A word on units, and it is good news. Frequencies are dimensionless and must sum to one. No S I units anywhere in this subtopic. Nothing to convert.
So the only sanity checks you need are on the board. P plus q equals one, and p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one. If either fails, stop and find the slip.
Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium holds only under five idealising conditions, and there is a trick to learning them that makes the next section free.
The trick is on the board at the top. Each condition is simply an instruction to switch off one evolutionary force. They are not five unrelated rules. They are one rule, applied five times.

Condition one. Large population. Why? So that chance fluctuations, which we call genetic drift, are negligible. In a small population, luck alone moves frequencies around. Make it large and luck averages out.
Condition two. Random mating. No mate choice based on genotype. Everyone is equally likely to pair with anyone, which is what lets us multiply probabilities later in the derivation.
Condition three. No mutation. No new alleles created, and none converted into others. The set of alleles is closed.
Condition four. No gene flow, also called migration. No alleles entering the population and none leaving it. The population is sealed.
Condition five. No natural selection. No genotype out-reproduces another. Every genotype leaves the same average number of offspring, so nothing is favoured.
<curious> Now look at the whole list and hear what it is really saying. Break any one of these and the population evolves. Just one. That is a startlingly fragile equilibrium.

And that fragility is the honest lesson of the framework. Real populations rarely satisfy all five, which is exactly why evolution happens. Equilibrium is not the normal state of life. It is the imaginary state we measure life against.

Now the payoff for learning the conditions properly. The five factors that disturb equilibrium are the mirror image of the five conditions. Break a condition and you get a force. And these five are what we mean by evolution.

Factor one. Gene migration, or gene flow. Alleles added to or lost from a population shift its frequencies. One detail worth having: repeated migration makes this a steady force, not a one-off accident.
Factor two. Genetic drift. Random change in allele frequency purely by chance. The crucial qualifier: powerful in small populations — which is why condition one demanded a large one.
Drift has two named special cases, and N E E T loves both. Look at the red panel.
Founder effect. A few individuals leave and start a new population, carrying only a slice of the original gene pool. The new population is not a copy of the old. It is a random sample of it.
Bottleneck effect. A population crashes, and the survivors' frequencies differ from the original. Same mechanism, opposite story. Founder is a few leaving; bottleneck is most dying.
Factor three. Mutation. A slow, random source of brand-new alleles, and it carries a title: the ultimate origin of all variation. Everything selection works on came from here first.
Factor four. Genetic recombination. Crossing over at meiosis shuffles alleles into new combinations. Note the verb: it rearranges what already exists.

<excited> Factor five. Natural selection. Non-random survival and reproduction, the main directional force. Now the memory aid: Genes Drift, Mutate, Recombine, get Selected. Gene flow, drift, mutation, recombination, selection. Five words, in order, whenever the question says list them.
We have a baseline and a list of forces. Put them together and the principle stops being a description and becomes an instrument.
On the left, predicted: the p squared to two p q to q squared ratio. What a non-evolving population must show, calculated from nothing but the allele frequencies.
On the right, measured. The counts you find when you go out and score the genotypes in a real population. Real organisms, real numbers.
Then you compare the two. That is the whole method, and it fits in one arrow.
If there is no gap, no force is acting; the population is in equilibrium. The boring outcome, and also the rare one.

<excited> If there is a gap, one of the five forces is acting, and the size of the gap measures how much. That is why we bother with an unrealistic idealisation. Hardy-Weinberg becomes a detector of evolution. You cannot see the force, but you can see the discrepancy it leaves behind.

Now a precision note, for the careful student, because you will notice the problem yourself. Mutation and recombination mainly supply variation. Strictly, recombination reshuffles existing alleles and does not by itself change allele frequencies at all.
So there is a small tension. N C E R T lists all five as factors affecting equilibrium, and that is the exam-expected answer. Write all five when asked. Do not get clever in the hall.

But hold the truth alongside it. Selection and drift actually push frequencies in a direction. Mutation and recombination load the gun; selection and drift aim it. Know the exam answer, and know why it simplifies.
A three-mark C B S E derivation, in five short steps. Do not memorise it. Follow it once and you never will.
Set up. Two alleles: A with frequency p, a with frequency q. Because there are only two, p plus q equals one. That is all we assume.
Step one. Gametes carry alleles in the same proportion. Each carries exactly one allele, so the fraction of sperm carrying A is p, and carrying a is q. Same for eggs.
Why it matters, because most students skip it: it lets us treat fertilisation as drawing one allele from a sperm pool and one from an egg pool. Reproduction has become a probability problem.
Step two. Random mating means random union of gametes: any sperm is equally likely to meet any egg. When events are independent, we may multiply their frequencies. That is why condition two exists.
So look at the Punnett square. Along the top, the egg pool. Down the side, the sperm pool. Four boxes, each a product.
Step three. Collect the genotypes. A A forms one way. Small a a forms one way. But A a forms two ways — look at the square, A a appears in two boxes.
<excited> That is where the factor of two comes from. Not a rule someone invented — a count of boxes. So A A equals p squared, A a equals two p q, a a equals q squared.
Step four. These genotypes are the whole population, so their frequencies sum to one. And notice what that expression is: the binomial expansion of p plus q, all squared. Which is one.
Before the toolkit, we owe the derivation its last step — the one that explains the word equilibrium.

Step five. Why does it stay there? If nothing removes or adds alleles, p and q are unchanged next generation. Same multiplication, same genotype frequencies. The pattern regenerates forever. That unchanging state is Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
Now the toolkit. This board is the whole subtopic compressed into two equations. And the discipline is: always know which one you are holding.
Top left. For the two alleles: p plus q equals one. Two alleles, two frequencies, accounting for all of them.
Top right. For the three genotypes: p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one. Three genotypes, three frequencies, accounting for all of them.
Same logic, different objects. One counts alleles, the other organisms. Mixing them is not a small error: the arithmetic still runs, quietly wrong.

So here is the labelling habit that fixes it. P squared is A A, the dominant homozygotes. Two p q is A a, the carriers. Q squared is a a, the recessive phenotype — the only one you can see from outside.
<curious> That last one is the door into every numerical. Q squared is the only term you can count in the field without a genetic test. Everything else is reached from it.

And the units, once more, because it is free marks. Frequencies are dimensionless. No S I units here at all. The only checks you need are p plus q equals one and p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one. Run both, every time, before you commit.
Selection एक चीज़ नहीं है। इसके तीन स्वाद हैं, और exam आपसे किसी description या graph से इन्हें पहचानने को कहता है। तो इन्हें आकार की तरह सीखिए।
पहले तस्वीर सेट कीजिए। Vertical axis पर number of individuals और horizontal पर phenotype लगाइए। आपको bell curve मिलती है। Selection उस curve का आकार बदलता है, और हर type अलग तरह से बदलता है।
तीनों panels देखिए। Dashed curve पहले की है। Solid curve बाद की। Shaded हिस्सा वो है जो selection ने हटा दिया।

Panel एक, stabilising selection. ये average को favour करता है और दोनों extremes हटा देता है। तो peak ऊँची और पतली हो जाती है। कुछ भी बग़ल में नहीं खिसकता। Population बस आपस में ज़्यादा एक जैसी हो जाती है।
Quote करने वाला example है human birth weight का mean के आसपास सिमटना। बहुत छोटे और बहुत बड़े, दोनों बच्चों का हाल बुरा रहा, तो बीच वाला दोनों तरफ़ से जीत गया।
Panel दो, directional selection. ये एक extreme को favour करता है, तो पूरी peak उसी extreme की तरफ़ खिसक जाती है। तीर देखिए। Curve पतली नहीं होती, वो चलती है।
Example है soot से काले हुए शहरों में गहरे रंग के peppered moths. Soot ने हल्के moths को शिकारियों को दिखा दिया, तो population काले की तरफ़ कूच कर गई। एक दिशा, एक खिसकाव।

ऊपर बायाँ box. दो alleles के लिए: p plus q equals one. दो alleles, दो frequencies, और उन्हें सबका हिसाब देना है।
ऊपर दायाँ box. तीन genotypes के लिए: p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one. तीन genotypes, तीन frequencies, और उन्हें सबका हिसाब देना है।
वही तर्क, अलग चीज़ें। एक alleles गिनती है, दूसरी जीव। इन्हें मिला देना छोटी ग़लती नहीं है, क्योंकि ये अलग क़िस्म की संख्याएँ देती हैं और arithmetic फिर भी चुपचाप ग़लत चलती रहती है।
तो ये रही वो labelling की आदत जो इसे ठीक करती है। P squared है A A, dominant homozygotes. Two p q है A a, यानी carriers. और q squared है a a, recessive phenotype, इकलौता जो आप बाहर से देख सकते हैं।

<curious> आख़िरी वाले पर ठहरना बनता है, क्योंकि यही हर numerical का दरवाज़ा है। Q squared इकलौता term है जिसे आप बिना genetic test के मैदान में गिन सकते हैं। Toolkit की बाक़ी हर चीज़ वहीं से पहुँची जाती है।

और units, एक बार और, क्योंकि ये मुफ़्त के marks हैं। Frequencies dimensionless हैं। इस subtopic में कोई S I unit है ही नहीं। आपको बस p plus q equals one और p squared plus two p q plus q squared equals one चाहिए। दोनों चलाइए, हर बार, जवाब पक्का करने से पहले।

sections.title: Q1 [CBSE Board, 3 marks] — state the princ... & Cousins, not ancestors...

board_events.text: Q1 — State the Hardy-Weinberg principle and list any three factors that can disturb genetic equilibrium.
Three marks, three demands. Read the question as a checklist.

board_events.caption: What the marking scheme is looking for
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"><defs><marker id="m1" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#2563eb"/></marker><marker id="m2" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#059669"/></marker><marker id="m3" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#dc2626"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="360" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="320" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Q1 — CBSE (3 marks): what the marking scheme wants</text>
<rect x="18" y="42" width="604" height="44" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">"State the Hardy–Weinberg principle and list any THREE factors</text>
<text x="320" y="80" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">that can disturb genetic equilibrium."</text>
<rect x="18" y="100" width="604" height="76" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="44" cy="124" r="13" fill="#2563eb"/><text x="44" y="129" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">1</text>
<text x="68" y="122" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">The CONSTANCY statement</text>
<text x="68" y="142" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">"In a large, randomly-mating population free from mutation, gene flow and selection,</text>
<text x="68" y="160" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">allele frequencies remain constant from generation to generation."</text>
<rect x="18" y="184" width="604" height="60" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="44" cy="208" r="13" fill="#059669"/><text x="44" y="213" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">2</text>
<text x="68" y="206" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">The EQUATION</text>
<rect x="240" y="212" width="180" height="26" rx="5" fill="#d1fae5"/>
<text x="330" y="231" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">p² + 2pq + q² = 1</text>
<rect x="430" y="212" width="120" height="26" rx="5" fill="#d1fae5"/>
<text x="490" y="231" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">p + q = 1</text>
<rect x="18" y="252" width="604" height="60" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="2"/>
<circle cx="44" cy="276" r="13" fill="#d97706"/><text x="44" y="281" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="bold" fill="#ffffff">3</text>
<text x="68" y="274" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#d97706">ANY THREE valid factors</text>
<rect x="68" y="284" width="128" height="22" rx="11" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#d97706"/><text x="132" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">gene flow</text>
<rect x="204" y="284" width="128" height="22" rx="11" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#d97706"/><text x="268" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">genetic drift</text>
<rect x="340" y="284" width="128" height="22" rx="11" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#d97706"/><text x="404" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">natural selection</text>
<rect x="476" y="284" width="140" height="22" rx="11" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="546" y="300" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#475569">mutation / recombination</text>
<rect x="18" y="318" width="604" height="26" rx="8" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="336" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Three demands, three marks. Statement WITHOUT the equation caps you at two.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Demand 1 — the CONSTANCY statement: in a large, randomly-mating population free from mutation, gene flow and selection, allele frequencies remain constant from generation to generation.
Demand 2 — the EQUATION: genotype frequencies follow $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$, where $p + q = 1$.
Demand 3 — ANY THREE disturbing factors: gene flow (migration), genetic drift, and natural selection. Also acceptable: mutation, genetic recombination.
Why it scores: it gives the constancy statement, the equation, and names valid factors — the three things the marking scheme requires.
The commonest way to lose a mark here is to state the principle beautifully and never write the equation.
Habit: the words 'state the Hardy-Weinberg principle' should make your pen write the sentence AND both equations, without being asked.
Q2 — Weismann's experiment of cutting the tails of mice for 22 generations was designed to test, and ultimately refute, which claim?
(a) Natural selection  (b) Inheritance of acquired characters  (c) Saltation  (d) Genetic drift

board_events.caption: One question kills three options
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"><defs><marker id="m1" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#2563eb"/></marker><marker id="m2" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#059669"/></marker><marker id="m3" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#dc2626"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="360" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="320" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Q2 — CUET: what was the experiment TESTING?</text>
<rect x="18" y="42" width="604" height="44" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">"Weismann’s experiment of cutting the tails of mice for 22 generations was designed</text>
<text x="320" y="80" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">to test, and ultimately refute, which claim?"</text>
<rect x="18" y="98" width="604" height="52" rx="8" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="118" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">One question decides it: what KIND of thing is a cut tail?</text>
<text x="320" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">A cut tail is an ACQUIRED modification of the BODY. So the item is about inheritance of the body.</text>
<rect x="18" y="164" width="290" height="34" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/>
<text x="32" y="186" font-size="12" fill="#475569">(a) Natural selection</text>
<path d="M240 173 L282 191 M240 191 L282 173" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<rect x="18" y="204" width="290" height="34" rx="6" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="3"/>
<text x="32" y="226" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">(b) Inheritance of acquired characters</text>
<rect x="332" y="164" width="290" height="34" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/>
<text x="346" y="186" font-size="12" fill="#475569">(c) Saltation</text>
<path d="M554 173 L596 191 M554 191 L596 173" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<rect x="332" y="204" width="290" height="34" rx="6" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/>
<text x="346" y="226" font-size="12" fill="#475569">(d) Genetic drift</text>
<path d="M554 213 L596 231 M554 231 L596 213" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.5"/>
<rect x="18" y="252" width="604" height="46" rx="8" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="272" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Why the other three die together</text>
<text x="320" y="290" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">(a), (c) and (d) are all about VARIATION and FREQUENCY CHANGE — not about inheriting bodily modifications.</text>
<rect x="18" y="308" width="604" height="34" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="330" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">No tail-less offspring, ever → acquired body changes are NOT inherited → Lamarckism falls. Answer: (b)</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Answer: (b) Inheritance of acquired characters.
Fast reasoning: cutting tails is an acquired modification of the BODY. If tail-less offspring never appear, then acquired body changes are not inherited — the central claim of Lamarckism.
Why the other three die together: (a), (c) and (d) all concern variation and frequency change, NOT the inheritance of bodily modifications.
So they are irrelevant to what the experiment actually tests.
The technique: ask what KIND of thing the experiment manipulated. A cut tail is somatoplasm — so the item can only be about inheriting body changes.
Hold the number: 22 generations. And the result is not 'few tail-less mice' — it is NOT ONE, ever.
Q3 — In a large, randomly-mating coastal town of 10,000 people, 400 show a recessive trait. Find the allele frequencies and the expected number of carriers.
Entry point: the recessive phenotype count gives you $q^2$ directly.

board_events.caption: Root first, then everything follows
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"><defs><marker id="m1" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#2563eb"/></marker><marker id="m2" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#059669"/></marker><marker id="m3" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#dc2626"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="360" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="320" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Q3 — NEET numerical: one number unlocks everything</text>
<rect x="18" y="42" width="604" height="38" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="60" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Coastal town of 10,000 people. 400 show a recessive trait. Large, randomly mating.</text>
<text x="320" y="74" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Find the allele frequencies and the expected number of carriers.</text>
<rect x="18" y="92" width="140" height="60" rx="8" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/>
<text x="88" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">ENTRY POINT</text>
<text x="88" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">recessive shown</text>
<text x="88" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">= q²</text>
<path d="M162 122 L188 122" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#m1)"/>
<rect x="194" y="92" width="140" height="60" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="264" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">STEP 1</text>
<text x="264" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">q² = 400 / 10000</text>
<text x="264" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">= 0.04</text>
<path d="M338 122 L364 122" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#m1)"/>
<rect x="370" y="92" width="120" height="60" rx="8" fill="#fef3c7" stroke="#d97706" stroke-width="3"/>
<text x="430" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#d97706">STEP 2 — ROOT IT</text>
<text x="430" y="132" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">q = √0.04</text>
<text x="430" y="148" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">= 0.2</text>
<path d="M494 122 L520 122" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#m1)"/>
<rect x="526" y="92" width="96" height="60" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="574" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">STEP 3</text>
<text x="574" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">p = 1 − q</text>
<text x="574" y="146" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">= 0.8</text>
<rect x="18" y="166" width="604" height="60" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="186" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">STEP 4 — read off every genotype</text>
<rect x="46" y="194" width="170" height="24" rx="5" fill="#dbeafe"/>
<text x="131" y="211" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">AA: p² = 0.64 → 6400</text>
<rect x="236" y="194" width="170" height="24" rx="5" fill="#fef3c7"/>
<text x="321" y="211" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Aa: 2pq = 0.32 → 3200</text>
<rect x="426" y="194" width="170" height="24" rx="5" fill="#fee2e2"/>
<text x="511" y="211" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">aa: q² = 0.04 → 400</text>
<rect x="18" y="238" width="290" height="46" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="163" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">SANITY CHECK — always</text>
<text x="163" y="276" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">6400 + 3200 + 400 = 10000 ✓   0.64 + 0.32 + 0.04 = 1 ✓</text>
<rect x="332" y="238" width="290" height="46" rx="8" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="477" y="258" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">ANSWER</text>
<text x="477" y="276" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">q = 0.2, p = 0.8, carriers = 3200</text>
<rect x="18" y="296" width="604" height="46" rx="8" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/>
<text x="320" y="316" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">THE KEY MOVE: the recessive phenotype count gives you q² DIRECTLY. Always take the square root first.</text>
<text x="320" y="334" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Students who treat 0.04 as q get every single subsequent number wrong.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Homozygous dominant: $p^2 = 0.64 \Rightarrow 6400$.
KEY MOVE: always take the square root FIRST. Students who treat $0.04$ as $q$ get every subsequent number wrong.
Q4 — 1000 plants show AA = 300, Aa = 500, aa = 200. Find the allele frequencies, then decide whether the population is in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.
This one gives you GENOTYPE COUNTS, not a phenotype fraction. So you cannot start from $q^2$ — you must count alleles.

board_events.caption: Count alleles, predict, compare
board_events.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 360" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif"><defs><marker id="m1" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#2563eb"/></marker><marker id="m2" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#059669"/></marker><marker id="m3" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L6 3 L0 6 z" fill="#dc2626"/></marker></defs><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="360" fill="#f8fafc"/><text x="320" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Q4 — NEET High-Difficulty: is it in equilibrium?</text>
<rect x="18" y="42" width="604" height="36" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">1000 plants: AA = 300, Aa = 500, aa = 200. Find p and q, then decide.</text>
<rect x="18" y="88" width="290" height="96" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="3"/>
<text x="163" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">Step 1 — COUNT THE ALLELES</text>
<text x="163" y="128" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Each AA plant carries TWO A alleles.</text>
<text x="163" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Each Aa plant carries ONE.</text>
<rect x="40" y="152" width="246" height="24" rx="5" fill="#fee2e2"/>
<text x="163" y="169" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">A alleles = 2(AA) + Aa, NOT AA + Aa</text>
<rect x="332" y="88" width="290" height="96" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="477" y="108" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#2563eb">Step 2 — the arithmetic</text>
<text x="477" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">p = [2(300) + 500] / 2(1000)</text>
<text x="477" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">= 1100 / 2000 = 0.55</text>
<text x="477" y="172" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">q = 1 − 0.55 = 0.45</text>
<rect x="18" y="194" width="604" height="96" rx="8" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="320" y="214" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">Step 3 — compare OBSERVED against EXPECTED</text>
<rect x="40" y="224" width="180" height="26" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#94a3b8"/>
<text x="130" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Genotype</text>
<rect x="220" y="224" width="180" height="26" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#94a3b8"/>
<text x="310" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Observed</text>
<rect x="400" y="224" width="200" height="26" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#94a3b8"/>
<text x="500" y="242" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Expected</text>
<rect x="40" y="250" width="180" height="20" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="130" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">AA (p²N)</text>
<rect x="220" y="250" width="180" height="20" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="310" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">300</text>
<rect x="400" y="250" width="200" height="20" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="500" y="265" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">0.3025 × 1000 = 302.5</text>
<rect x="40" y="270" width="180" height="20" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="130" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">Aa (2pqN)</text>
<rect x="220" y="270" width="180" height="20" fill="#ffffff" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="310" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">500</text>
<rect x="400" y="270" width="200" height="20" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#94a3b8"/><text x="500" y="285" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">0.495 × 1000 = 495</text>
<rect x="18" y="298" width="290" height="44" rx="8" fill="#d1fae5" stroke="#059669" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="163" y="316" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">aa: observed 200 vs expected 202.5</text>
<text x="163" y="334" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#059669">Almost identical → approximately in equilibrium</text>
<rect x="332" y="298" width="290" height="44" rx="8" fill="#fee2e2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2"/>
<text x="477" y="316" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="bold" fill="#dc2626">THE TRAP</text>
<text x="477" y="334" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">Forgetting that each heterozygote contributes ONE A allele.</text>
</svg>

board_events.text: Each AA plant carries TWO A alleles; each Aa plant carries ONE. So A alleles $= 2(AA) + Aa$, NOT $AA + Aa$.
Expected counts under equilibrium: $p^2 N = 0.3025 \times 1000 = 302.5$; $2pqN = 0.495 \times 1000 = 495$; $q^2 N = 0.2025 \times 1000 = 202.5$.
Compare: observed 300 / 500 / 200 versus expected 302.5 / 495 / 202.5.
Almost identical → the population is APPROXIMATELY in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium; no major evolutionary force appears to be acting.
Note the word 'approximately'. Real data never lands exactly on the prediction, and the examiner does not expect it to.
The five ways students lose this subtopic
1. Confusing ALLELE frequencies with GENOTYPE frequencies. $p + q = 1$ is for alleles; $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$ is for genotypes. Label each number as you write it.
2. Forgetting to square-root. When a question gives the recessive phenotype fraction, that is $q^2$, not $q$. Take the root FIRST.
3. Dropping the two in $2pq$. The heterozygote forms two ways — the factor of two is not optional.
4. Treating Lamarckism as totally wrong. It is RIGHT that use and disuse change the body; it is WRONG that those changes are inherited. Be precise in distinction questions.
5. Listing 'random mating' as a disturbing factor. Random mating is a CONDITION for equilibrium; it is NON-random mating that disturbs it.
Pitfalls two and three are pure arithmetic. Pitfalls one, four and five are pure reading.
Every one of these has a distractor built for it somewhere in the paper.
The wrong options are not random numbers. They are exactly the answers these five mistakes produce.
One number unlocks the whole question
The recessive phenotype is your entry point — it equals $q^2$.

board_events.text: NEET almost always asks one question here — overwhelmingly a chronological-sequence item, or a brain-capacity / feature match.
CUET likes single-fact recall: who used fire, which had the largest brain. CBSE may ask a short 'trends in human evolution' answer.
But this is the part of the chapter where students most often carry a wrong picture: a tidy single-file parade of a stooping ape gradually straightening up into a businessman.
Two things are wrong with that image. Fixing them is most of the battle.
Wrong thing one: we did not descend from chimpanzees. Wrong thing two: evolution was not a straight march of steady improvement.
What looks in a textbook like a neat sequence is really a PRUNED TREE drawn as a line.
We did not descend from monkeys or chimpanzees
Chimps are not our ancestors. They are our cousins.
